steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Refracting telescopes use a convex objective lens to gather and focus light

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Reflecting telescopes use a concave primary mirror; Newtonian and Cassegrain are common designs

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Magnification = focal length of objective / focal length of eyepiece

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Resolving power is the ability to distinguish fine detail; larger apertures give better resolution

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What are the advantages of reflecting telescopes over refracting? | Q: How is magnification calculated? | Q: Why are radio telescopes often very large?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Reflectors: no chromatic aberration, easier to make large mirrors (no internal defects), mirrors can be supported from behind, and are cheaper for the same aperture. | Magnification = focal length of objective ÷ focal length of eyepiece. | Radio wavelengths are much longer than visible light, so larger dishes are needed to achieve similar resolving power (resolution ∝ aperture/wavelength).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Magnification formula is often tested — know M = f_obj / f_eye Reflectors solve chromatic aberration — this is the #1 advantage Space telescopes: no atmosphere = no distortion + access to blocked wavelengths Both boards test telescope types and their comparative advantages
